title: Grading on three axes
teaches: Grade your trading on the three things trading coach Brett Steenbarger grades every day: the idea, how you traded it, and your preparation. Never grade one trade by its P&L, since good trades lose and bad trades win; only many trades taken the same way show whether the setup works.

sources.title: How to Conduct a Professional Review of Your Trading (video and transcript: Mike Bellafiore, Dr. Brett Steenbarger, Max Ganik, 2020-11-19)
sources.why_reliable: SMB Capital is a New York proprietary trading firm; co-founder Mike Bellafiore wrote One Good Trade (Wiley) and The PlayBook (FT Press). In this video Brett Steenbarger, Ph.D. (named in the contract's Tier 2 list of trading authors) describes his own daily review in his own words. The page's transcript is machine-made (it prints 'training' for 'trading' and 'stevenbarger'), so quotes are taken only from stretches that read cleanly, and the one with 'training' is flagged in its claim.

facts.quote: grading your ideas means you’re evaluating the idea behind your trade
facts.claim: Steenbarger's first grade is on the idea: you judge the idea behind the trade.

facts.quote: did i trade an idea that genuinely had an edge behind it or perhaps did i get a bias during my trading was i unduly influenced by a particular flow in the market or a particular piece of news
facts.claim: The idea grade asks whether the trade had a genuine edge, or whether a bias, a market flow or a piece of news pulled you in.

facts.quote: grading that you’re trading the idea i am separating out the idea generation
facts.claim: Steenbarger grades how he traded an idea separately from the idea itself.

facts.quote: how well did i enter did i enter with truly good risk reward or did i end up chasing the trade and wind up with poor risk reward how was my sizing of the position
facts.claim: The trading grade asks if the entry gave good reward for the risk or chased into poor reward for the risk, and how the position was sized.

facts.quote: how did i manage the position while it was on and finally the exit
facts.claim: The trading grade also covers how you managed the position and how you exited.

facts.quote: that personal preparation includes time spent in the morning pre-market for exercise physical exercise reviewing markets reviewing the previous day’s trading
facts.claim: Steenbarger's preparation covers his morning before the open: exercise, reviewing the markets and reviewing the previous day's trading.

facts.quote: every single day i’m getting at least three grades for the quality of the ideas that day for the training of those ideas and for my preparation
facts.claim: Steenbarger gives himself at least three grades a day: the quality of his ideas, how he traded them, and his preparation.

facts.quote: if you have made decisions based on all those criteria that’s an a trade even if that particular trade didn’t happen to be profitable on that occasion
facts.claim: On SMB's review panel: a trade made on all your checklist criteria is an A trade, even if that one lost money.

facts.quote: i had a great entry on a trade today it was really good
facts.claim: Steenbarger's own example starts with a great entry.

facts.quote: i definitely should have taken profits earlier it went against me and i ended up making some money but not nearly what i should have
facts.claim: He botched the exit: he made some money, but not nearly what he should have.

facts.quote: probably our highest p l trader had trouble pulling the trigger on his trades but we said hey you’re really terrific at developing ideas
facts.claim: SMB's example: probably their highest-P&L trader had terrific ideas, and his problem was pulling the trigger on them.

facts.quote: Yet a further refinement is to conduct separate reviews of the various facets of trading
facts.claim: Steenbarger reviews the different parts of trading separately.

facts.quote: How well did you develop sound ideas to trade?
facts.claim: One separate review: how well you developed sound ideas.

facts.quote: How well did you enter positions and achieve favorable reward relative to risk?
facts.claim: Another: how well you entered and got good reward for the risk you took.

facts.quote: How well did you scale into and/or out of positions to optimize profitability and manage risk?
facts.claim: Another: how well you scaled in and out of positions to manage profit and risk.

facts.quote: How well did you manage yourself during the trade--and throughout the day--to sustain optimal focus and keep yourself in a peak performing state?
facts.claim: Another: how well you managed yourself to stay focused through the day.

facts.quote: The first review occurs at the start of trading where you examine how your markets or stocks are setting up
facts.claim: The first review of the day comes before trading: how your markets and stocks are setting up.

facts.quote: Just as a tennis player will work on different aspects of her or his game (the serve; backhand; net game; etc.), we view and review different facets of trading
facts.claim: Like a tennis player working on separate parts of the game, you review and work on separate parts of trading.

facts.quote: he graded himself at the end of the day purely on process grounds: how well he generated ideas; how well he structured trades based on the ideas; how well he managed those positions and their associated risk
facts.claim: A portfolio manager Steenbarger coached graded each day purely on process: his ideas, how he structured trades from them, and how he managed the risk.

facts.quote: The goal was to achieve consistently high process scores at the end of trading days, whether those days had positive P/L or not.
facts.claim: The goal was high process scores whether the day's P&L was positive or not.

facts.quote: My trading day begins early in the morning with an assessment of overseas markets, an advance look at economic reports due for the day, a review of the prior day's market indicators
facts.claim: Steenbarger's morning includes an advance look at the economic reports due that day.

facts.quote: Subjects rated the thinking as better, rated the decision maker as more competent, or indicated greater willingness to yield the decision when the outcome was favorable than when it was unfavorable.
facts.claim: In the study, people rated the thinking behind a decision as better when its outcome was favorable.

facts.quote: Since good decisions can lead to bad outcomes (and vice versa) decision makers cannot infallibly be graded by their results.
facts.claim: Good decisions can lead to bad outcomes and bad ones to good outcomes, so decisions can't be reliably graded by their results.

facts.quote: Information that is available only after a decision is made is irrelevant to the quality of the decision.
facts.claim: What you learn only after a decision has no bearing on how good the decision was.

facts.quote: When decisions turn out badly, it may sometimes be useful to reanalyze them from the decision maker's viewpoint at the time of the decision
facts.claim: When a decision turns out badly, re-check it from where the decision maker stood at the time.

facts.quote: Mere understanding that such confusion contaminates these evaluations is not enough to eliminate it.
facts.claim: Knowing that outcomes distort your judgment is not enough to stop it.

facts.quote: People who judge their own behavior well or badly as a function of its outcome may hold themselves responsible for both good and bad luck, becoming smug in their success or self-reproachful in their failure.
facts.claim: Grading yourself by outcomes can make you take credit and blame for luck: smug after wins, hard on yourself after losses.

facts.quote: information can operate only within a sequence of similar decisions, not in a single decision.
facts.claim: Outcomes can update your read on the odds only across a run of similar decisions, not from one.

facts.quote: In poker you can win with the worst hand. You can lose with the best hand.
facts.claim: Annie Duke: in poker you can win with the worst hand and lose with the best.

facts.quote: So if all I know is that Taylor and Morgan played poker for an hour and Taylor won, I know very little about the quality of the underlying decisions.
facts.claim: Knowing only who won an hour of poker tells you very little about the quality of the decisions.

facts.quote: That means if I only know one thing about the chess game, which is that Taylor beat Morgan, then I know Taylor made better decisions relative to Morgan.
facts.claim: In chess, knowing who won tells you who made the better decisions.

facts.quote: But almost no decisions you make in life are actually of that type. They’re much more poker-like
facts.claim: Duke: almost no real decisions are like chess; they are much more like poker.

facts.quote: We assume an allocator whose investments win at the end of the year must be a better decision-maker than someone whose investments lost, despite the fact that the data does not necessarily bear that out.
facts.claim: People assume the investor whose bets won this year decided better, even when the data does not show it.

facts.quote: when we get a bad result, we forget that there was an influence of luck on the outcome. And we tie the quality of the result back to the quality of the decision.
facts.claim: Resulting: after a bad result we forget the luck and tie the quality of the result back to the quality of the decision.

facts.quote: if I'm playing poker and I win a single hand of poker, it doesn't really tell you very much about what the quality of my decision-making in that single hand was.
facts.claim: Winning one hand of poker tells you little about how good the decisions in that hand were.

facts.quote: But if I play enough poker, the outcome in the aggregate over time will start to tell you something about how good I am at poker.
facts.claim: Over enough hands, the results taken together start to show how good the player is.

facts.quote: I'm putting you into my situation at the time that I had to make the decision.
facts.claim: Duke reviews a hand by putting the listener where she stood when she had to decide.

facts.quote: if I tell you any of that stuff, you're going to naturally fit the narrative to what actually ended up happening in the hand.
facts.claim: Tell the reviewer how it ended and they will fit their story to the ending.

facts.quote: The outcome certainly tells you more and more and more the more skill there is in what you're doing.
facts.claim: The more a result depends on skill, the more one result tells you.

facts.quote: they ban discussion of how it turned out for them. ANNIE: Well, for smart poker players, they do, for sure.
facts.claim: Duke: smart poker players ban talk of how a hand turned out when they discuss what they should have done.

facts.quote: The reactions reveal a common decision trap — judging the quality of a decision by relying on the quality of its outcome, despite the significant intervening element of luck in the way any decision turns out.
facts.claim: Duke: a common trap is judging a decision by its outcome, ignoring the luck in how any decision turns out.

facts.quote: People make good decisions and experience bad outcomes. And good outcomes can result from very bad decisions.
facts.claim: Good decisions can end badly, and very bad decisions can end well.

facts.quote: some good decisions should never be repeated and some bad decisions should be reinforced.
facts.claim: Resulting can make you believe some good decisions should never be repeated and some bad ones should be reinforced.

facts.quote: There’s a lot of noise in decision quality and outcomes. That allows for biases to dig in — like resulting, which means deriving quality from one instance.
facts.claim: Resulting means deriving a decision's quality from one instance.

facts.quote: These were two similarly unexpected, creative, and mathematically well-reasoned play-calls. Two different outcomes.
facts.claim: Duke calls the Pete Carroll pass a mathematically well-reasoned call that happened to have a bad outcome.

facts.quote: In the 2015 Super Bowl, Seattle Seahawks coach Pete Carroll also made an against-all-expectations call on the one-yard line. Despite the levels of sophisticated thinking behind the play, it failed, leading to an interception and victory by the Patriots.
facts.claim: In the 2015 Super Bowl, Pete Carroll's pass call at the one-yard line was intercepted and the Patriots won.

facts.quote: With 26 seconds left at the end of the fourth quarter, the Seahawks were on the New England Patriot’s 1-yard line. It was second-down, the Seahawks were down by four points, and had one timeout.
facts.claim: Seattle was on the Patriots' 1-yard line, down four, with 26 seconds left and one timeout.

facts.quote: Annie notes that the probability of a short-pass interception is below two percent, based on 15 years of NFL data.
facts.claim: The show's write-up says Duke puts a short-pass interception below two percent, from 15 years of NFL data (not cited: retellings of the book differ).

facts.quote: Moreover, if the pass is incomplete, the clock stops on its own.
facts.claim: An incomplete pass would have stopped the clock.

facts.quote: On the flip side, when judging ourselves, we engage in a self-serving bias. If it’s a really good outcome, it’s because we’re awesome. When it’s a bad outcome, we want it to not be our fault.
facts.claim: Judging ourselves, we take credit for good outcomes and duck the blame for bad ones.

facts.quote: The problem with resulting is that too often people look at bad outcomes and conclude it was caused by a bad decision process
facts.claim: Resulting: blaming a bad outcome on a bad decision process.

facts.quote: Conversely, it could be that one concludes a good outcome was the result of a sound process—when it was just luck
facts.claim: The other half: crediting a good outcome to a sound process when it was just luck.

facts.quote: Losing a trade with a good process can’t be defined as a step backward. Realistically, making money with bad process would be a step backwards
facts.claim: Tendler: a loss with good process is not a step backward; making money with bad process is.

facts.quote: Yes, money is the scoreboard in trading, but it is not reliable for measuring performance in the short-term.
facts.claim: Money is the scoreboard, but it does not measure performance reliably over the short term.

facts.quote: this trader should instead be looking at PnL over a larger timeframe, like three to six months
facts.claim: Tendler would judge P&L over a longer stretch, like three to six months.

facts.quote: Were my entries, stops, and exits performed effectively?
facts.claim: Schwab's trade review asks whether your entries, stops and exits were carried out well.

facts.quote: Plan for the week ahead: Identify potential news events relevant to your portfolio like earnings announcements, dividends, or major economic news.
facts.claim: Schwab's weekly prep looks ahead for earnings, dividends and major economic news.

facts.quote: Start with the difference between the entry price, $67, and the exit price, $57, or $10
facts.claim: Risk per share is the entry price minus the stop (exit) price: $67 minus $57 is $10.

facts.quote: Losing streaks can happen to the best of us, but sometimes a bout of bad luck can actually reflect a problem with our trading strategy.
facts.claim: A losing streak can be bad luck, or it can point to a real problem with the strategy.

facts.quote: To begin, traders should look at whether they're losing or making money on a net basis, then look for patterns in their wins and losses.
facts.claim: To tell which, check whether you make or lose money net, then look for patterns in the wins and losses.

facts.quote: he would see the market moving away from his ideal entry point and, fearful of missing out on the opportunity, he would chase the short term movement
facts.claim: The portfolio manager's problem: when the market moved away from his entry, fear of missing out made him chase.

facts.quote: Turns out, Pete’s call wasn’t a bad one based on the facts he had. The interception was highly unlikely
facts.claim: The show's write-up of Duke's book: on the facts Carroll had, the call wasn't a bad one, and an interception was highly unlikely.

facts.quote: so he could have more confidence in being able to make those trades
facts.claim: SMB's aim with that trader: more confidence to make the trades his ideas called for.

facts.quote: And in terms of luck, there are no dice.
facts.claim: Duke: in chess there are no dice, so luck plays almost no part.

facts.quote: In terms of the hidden information, I can see my opponent's position.
facts.claim: Duke: in chess nothing is hidden; each player can see the other's position.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: UCT's rule: no new buys in the 3 days before earnings, and hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: UCT's rule: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Tired, sick, angry or distracted: no new trades that day.
facts.claim: UCT's rule: no new trades on a day you're tired, sick, angry or distracted.

facts.quote: Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.
facts.claim: UCT's rule: every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the open.

facts.quote: Journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally.
facts.claim: UCT's rule: journal every trade the same day and review the week every weekend, ideally.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: UCT's rule: every position has a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Each month, review the numbers: win rate, average win and loss in R, expectancy, and other statistics.
facts.claim: UCT's rule: each month, review the win rate, the average win and loss in R, and the expectancy.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk
facts.claim: UCT's rule: chasing costs size, not risk. The stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink.

walkthroughs.title: Three grades, every day
steps: Trading coach Brett Steenbarger gives himself at least three grades every trading day. Do the same.
First, your ideas. A real edge behind the trade, or just a bias or a headline pulling you in.
Second, how you traded it. A good entry or a chase, then the size, how you managed it, and the exit.
Third, your prep. His is exercise, a look at the markets, and a review of yesterday, all before the open.

walkthroughs.title: The result is not the grade
steps: In poker you can win with the worst hand and lose with the best. One trade works the same way.
Judging a decision by how it turned out is what Annie Duke calls resulting.
So grade what you did. Follow your whole plan and it's an A trade, even if it lost.

walkthroughs.title: When the results do count
steps: One trade tells you almost nothing. A pile of trades taken the same way starts to talk.
Money is the scoreboard, just not in the short run. Jared Tendler looks at three to six months.
So grade each trade on process. Let the pile judge the setup.

questions.q: Brett Steenbarger grades himself at least three ways every trading day. What's he grading?
choices: His ideas, his trading, his prep
Win rate, P&L and trade count
His entries, exits and profit
The market, the sector, the stock
questions.answer: His ideas, his trading, his prep
questions.why: His ideas, how he traded them, and his prep. Steenbarger is a trading coach, and he gives himself at least three grades every day. The idea grade asks if the trade had a real edge behind it. The trading grade covers the entry, the size, how he managed it and the exit. The prep grade is his work before the open: reviewing the markets and the day before. Notice what's missing. Not one of the three is the day's P&L. Split it up like this and you can see which part of your game is leaking.
questions.lesson_line: Three grades: the idea, how you traded it, and how ready you were. The P&L isn't one of them.

wrong.Win rate, P&L and trade count: Those are results and activity. His grades score his own work, not what the market paid him that day.
wrong.His entries, exits and profit: Entries and exits sit inside one grade, how he traded the idea. Profit isn't graded at all.
wrong.The market, the sector, the stock: That's a top-down way to pick trades. His grades look back at his own work.

questions.simple: Ideas, how he traded them, and prep. Each one gets its own grade, and none of them is the P&L.

questions.q: One trade's P&L tells you whether it was a good trade.
questions.why: False. One trade's P&L is a result, not a grade. Good decisions can end in bad outcomes, and bad ones can end well. In poker you can win with the worst hand and lose with the best. A single trade works the same way. Jared Tendler calls money the scoreboard, but not a reliable one in the short term. You'll have clean trades stop out and sloppy ones pay. So grade the trade on what you did: the idea, the entry, the stop, the size.
questions.lesson_line: The P&L is the result. The grade is how you did it.
questions.simple: False. Good trades can lose and bad ones can win, so one result tells you little about the trade.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Grading a decision by how it turned out is called ___.
questions.why: Resulting. It is Annie Duke's name for grading a decision by how it turned out. She calls it deriving quality from one instance. After a bad result you forget the luck and tie the result back to the decision.
questions.lesson_line: Resulting means grading the decision by the result. One trade is too noisy for that.
questions.simple: Resulting is the word, Annie Duke's name for judging a choice only by how it ended.

questions.q: You're giving last week's trade its idea grade, apart from how you traded it. What are you really asking?
choices: Was there a real edge in it?
Did it go up the next week?
Did I size and sell it well?
Was I ready before the open?
questions.answer: Was there a real edge in it?
questions.why: The edge. That's all the idea grade asks. Steenbarger checks if the trade had a genuine edge behind it. Or if a bias, a market flow or a piece of news pulled him in instead. The entry, the size and the sell belong to how you traded it. Being ready belongs to prep. Where the stock went the next week doesn't count either, because a real edge still loses some of the time. Be straight with yourself here. It was a setup on your plan, or it was a story you liked.
questions.lesson_line: The idea grade asks one thing: was there a real edge, or just a story I liked.

wrong.Was I ready before the open?: That's the third grade, your prep.
wrong.Did it go up the next week?: That's the outcome. A real edge can still lose, so next week's move can't grade the idea.
wrong.Did I size and sell it well?: That's the second grade, how you traded the idea. Keep it apart.

questions.simple: It asks if the trade had a real edge, not whether it worked or how well you sized and sold it.

questions.q: You're going over Tuesday's trades. Which of these goes under how you traded the idea?
choices: You chased it past your entry
The setup had no real edge
You skipped your morning review
It fell the day after you sold
questions.answer: You chased it past your entry
questions.why: The chase. How you traded the idea covers the entry, what you got paid for the risk, the size, the management and the exit. Steenbarger names chasing right in this grade, because it turns good reward for the risk into poor. And chasing costs you size. The stop stays where the chart put it, so the distance grows and you buy fewer shares. We don't buy more than 4% above the buy point for exactly that reason. A setup with no edge is an idea problem. A skipped morning review is prep. A drop after you sold isn't something you did at all.
questions.lesson_line: A good idea can still be traded badly. Grade the entry, size and exit on their own.

wrong.The setup had no real edge: That's the idea grade. You can trade a weak idea perfectly and it's still a weak idea.
wrong.It fell the day after you sold: You were already out. That's an outcome, not something you did.

questions.simple: Chasing goes under how you traded it. It's about your entry and what you got paid for the risk.

questions.q: Your own state counts in Steenbarger's grades, not just your read on the market.
questions.why: True. His prep grade includes physical exercise in the morning, along with reviewing the markets and the day before. On his blog he also grades how well you managed yourself through the day, to stay focused and at your best. So you get graded, not just your charts. We take that part seriously. Tired, sick, angry or distracted, we don't take new trades that day. Before the open, check how you feel as well as what the market's doing.
questions.lesson_line: Your own state is part of your prep. Grade it too.
questions.simple: True. His prep includes morning exercise, and he grades how well you kept your focus through the day.

questions.q: Annie Duke, the poker player, compares chess and poker. In which game does one win tell you more about the decisions?
choices: Chess, there's almost no luck
Poker, real money is at stake
Both tell you the same amount
Neither, one game never does
questions.why: Chess. Duke's point is simple. In chess there are no dice, and you can see your opponent's whole position. So if Taylor beat Morgan at chess, Taylor made the better decisions. In poker you can win with the worst hand, so one win tells you very little. The more skill decides a result, the more one result tells you. Here's why it matters to us. Duke says almost no real decisions are like chess. A trade is a poker hand.
questions.lesson_line: A trade is a hand of poker, not a game of chess. One hand tells you little.

wrong.Poker, real money is at stake: Money doesn't make a result more telling. With luck and hidden information, one poker win says little.
wrong.Both tell you the same amount: Duke's point is the opposite. The more skill decides a game, the more one result tells you.
wrong.Neither, one game never does: In chess it does. With no dice, the winner made the better decisions.

questions.simple: Chess, because there are no dice and nothing hidden, so the winner made the better decisions.

questions.q: In a 1988 study, people rated the thinking behind a decision higher when it happened to turn out well.
questions.why: True. In Baron and Hershey's study, people rated the thinking as better when the outcome was good. They even rated the person deciding as more competent. And they were judging someone else's decision, not their own. Duke sees the same thing in investing. We assume this year's winner decided better, even when the data doesn't show it. Your own grades can drift toward the P&L the same way. So watch for it, especially after a big green week.
questions.lesson_line: Grades drift toward the result. Watch for it in yours.
questions.simple: True. People judged the thinking as better when the result happened to be good.

questions.q: Steenbarger coached a portfolio manager who kept chasing. Finish the line on how he graded each day.
questions.sentence: He graded himself at the end of the day purely on ___ grounds.
questions.why: Process. He scored how well he generated ideas, structured trades from them and managed the risk. The goal was consistently high process scores, whether the day's P&L was positive or not. His problem had been chasing when the market moved away from his entry. Profit was not one of his scores.
questions.lesson_line: Score the work, green day or red.
questions.simple: Process is the word, since he scored how well he did the work, not whether the day made money.

questions.story: The setup checked every box on your written plan. You bought at your price, sized to plan, with your stop in. It hit the stop for your planned loss.
questions.q: How do you grade this one?
choices: A good trade that just lost
Bad trade, it lost real money
Good idea, but traded badly
Bad idea, since it didn't work
questions.answer: A good trade that just lost
questions.why: A good trade that just lost. You did everything your plan asked: the entry, the size, the stop. Make a trade on all of that and it's an A trade, even when that one doesn't pay. In poker you can lose with the best hand. Tendler goes further. Losing with good process isn't a step backward. So log it as an A and take the next one the same way. The loss is just the cost of doing business.
questions.lesson_line: A loss on a clean trade is the cost of doing business. I grade the work.

wrong.Bad idea, since it didn't work: A real edge still loses some of the time. One stop-out doesn't make the idea bad.
wrong.Bad trade, it lost real money: That's resulting, grading the decision by how it ended. A loss with good process isn't a step backward.
wrong.Good idea, but traded badly: Nothing says so. Entry, size and stop all went to plan.

questions.simple: A good trade that lost. You followed every rule, and a real edge still loses sometimes.

questions.story: Your plan is to buy tight setups in leading stocks. A headline gets you fired up, and you buy a stock that fits none of it. Your entry, stop and size follow your usual rules. It stops out.
questions.q: Which of your three grades comes out low?
choices: The idea behind it
How you traded it
Your preparation
None, losses happen
questions.why: The idea. Steenbarger's idea grade asks if the trade had a real edge, or if a piece of news pulled you in. Here the headline did. The stock fit nothing on your plan, so no edge from your plan stood behind it. You did trade it right. Entry, stop and size went by your rules, so that grade holds up. But clean execution can't rescue an idea that was never on your plan. It'd be the same low grade if it had worked. We write down every planned buy, with its entry, stop and size, before the open. A headline isn't on that list.
questions.lesson_line: Clean execution can't rescue an idea that was never in your plan.

wrong.How you traded it: Entry, stop and size followed your rules. That part you did right.
wrong.Your preparation: Nothing says you skipped your prep. The slip came when the headline hit.
wrong.None, losses happen: Losses do happen. But this one had no edge from your plan behind it, so it grades low, win or lose.

questions.simple: The idea grade is low. A headline pulled you into a stock your plan never called for.

questions.story: Your plan says this trade should not be held through earnings. You skip your weekly look ahead. You miss that the stock reports tonight, and it gaps down through your stop.
questions.q: Where did this one go wrong?
choices: Your preparation work
How you traded the stock
The idea, since it lost
None, it was just bad luck
questions.why: Your prep. That report date was knowable days ahead. A weekly look ahead is built to catch exactly this. Schwab's version checks for earnings, dividends and big economic news. Our rules on earnings are plain. No new buys in the 3 days before a report, and we only hold through one if the trade is up 5R. You held because you never saw the date. Which way it gapped was luck. Not knowing it was coming wasn't. Earnings dates are on the calendar in the UCT Terminal. Check it before you buy, and again in your weekend review.
questions.lesson_line: If you could have known it ahead of time, missing it isn't bad luck. It's prep.

wrong.How you traded the stock: Holding broke your plan only because you didn't know the date. The miss started earlier, in the look ahead you skipped.
wrong.The idea, since it lost: Losing money doesn't grade the idea. The miss was not knowing the report was due.
wrong.None, it was just bad luck: Which way the report moved it may be luck. Not knowing it was coming isn't. The date was knowable ahead of time.

questions.simple: Your prep. The earnings date was knowable, and a weekly look ahead would have shown it.

reasons: rebuilt around earnings to follow the owner's rulebook (C32 news days, B22 earnings)

questions.q: Plan: buy $50, stop $48, target $56. You chase and fill at $53, same stop and target. What do you get per $1 of risk now?
questions.why: $0.60. Work it from your real fill. The reward is $56 minus $53, so $3. The risk is $53 minus $48, so $5. $3 over $5 is $0.60 for every $1 you risk. At $50 the same plan paid $3.00 for every $1. The chart didn't change. Only your entry did. That's why Steenbarger grades chasing under how you traded the idea. And with the stop still at $48, the bigger risk per share means fewer shares. We don't buy more than 4% over the buy point, and $53 is past it.
questions.lesson_line: Chasing doesn't change the chart. It changes what you get paid for the risk.
questions.simple: Just $0.60. From $53 the target is closer to you than the stop is.

deeper.trap: A chase feels like the same trade because the chart looks the same. It isn't. The stop and the target stay put. Every dollar you pay over the plan moves you closer to the target and further from the stop. Here a $53 fill instead of $50 put the target closer than the stop. Grade that at the entry, even if the trade goes on to reach $56.

reasons: fill moved past the rulebook's chase line (C28)

wrong.$3.00: That's what the plan paid at your $50 entry, before you chased.
wrong.$1.67: Flipped. That's the risk over the reward.
wrong.$1.20: Mixed entries. You measured the reward from $50 but the risk from $53.

questions.q: Last week's trade is up for review. What should its idea grade rest on?
choices: What you knew at the entry
Where it closed a week later
How much the trade made or lost
News that came out after you sold
questions.answer: What you knew at the entry
questions.why: What you knew at the entry. Information you only get after a decision has nothing to do with how good the decision was. That comes straight from Baron and Hershey's study. So when a trade goes bad, go back to where you stood when you clicked. Duke reviews her poker hands the same way, from her seat at the moment she had to decide. Where it closed, what it made and the later news all came after. You couldn't have used any of it.
questions.lesson_line: Grade from your seat at the entry, not from where the chart sits now.

wrong.Where it closed a week later: That came after the decision. It tells you what happened, not how well you decided.
wrong.How much the trade made or lost: That's the result. Luck sits between the decision and the result.
wrong.News that came out after you sold: You couldn't have known it at the entry, so it can't grade the entry.

questions.simple: Grade it on what you knew when you bought. What you learn later can't make the choice better or worse.

questions.story: You buy a clean setup right at your entry. It reaches your target, where your plan says take profits. You hold for more instead. It fades, and you sell for a small gain.
questions.q: Which grade takes the hit?
choices: How you traded it, the exit
None, the trade made money
The idea, the gain was small
Your preparation that morning
questions.answer: How you traded it, the exit
questions.why: How you traded it, at the exit. The idea worked. It got to your target. Then you broke your own sell plan and gave most of it back. Steenbarger tells the same story about himself. A great entry, and he should have taken profits earlier. He made some money, just not nearly what he should have. So a green trade can still earn a low grade. Making money and doing it right aren't the same thing.
questions.lesson_line: A green trade can still earn a low grade. Making money isn't the same as doing it right.

wrong.None, the trade made money: That's grading by the result. You broke your exit plan, and the fade cost you most of the move.
wrong.The idea, the gain was small: The idea did its job. It reached your target. The gain shrank after that, at your exit.
wrong.Your preparation that morning: Nothing in the story points to your prep. The slip came at the exit.

questions.simple: How you traded it. Your plan said take profits at the target, and you held instead.

questions.q: Resulting means blaming a bad outcome on a bad decision. What's the other half of the trap?
choices: Calling a lucky win skill
Blaming luck for every loss
Trading smaller after a loss
Selling winners too early
questions.why: Calling a lucky win skill. Resulting cuts both ways. A bad outcome gets blamed on a bad process. A good outcome gets credited to a sound process when it was just luck. The second half is the sneaky one. Duke warns resulting can make you believe some bad decisions should be reinforced. Break a rule, get paid, call it skill, and you'll do it again. That's how a bad habit grows.
questions.lesson_line: A lucky win graded as skill gets repeated. That's how bad habits grow.

wrong.Blaming luck for every loss: That's a cousin bias: wins are skill, losses are bad luck. Resulting grades by the result either way.
wrong.Trading smaller after a loss: That's a reaction to losing, not a way of judging a decision.
wrong.Selling winners too early: That's an exit habit. Resulting is about how you judge a decision after the fact.

questions.simple: The other half is calling a lucky win skill. That can lead you to repeat a bad decision.

questions.q: Once you know about resulting, a trade's result stops swaying how you grade it.
questions.why: False. Knowing the bias doesn't switch it off. Baron and Hershey found that just understanding it is not enough to remove it. Tell someone how a hand ended and they'll fit the story to the ending. That's why smart poker players ban talk of how a hand turned out when they review it. Do the same with your trades. Journal each trade the same day, and write the grade before you look at the P&L.
questions.lesson_line: Knowing the bias won't save you. I write the grade before I look at the P&L.
questions.simple: False. Knowing about the bias doesn't switch it off, so hide the result while you grade.

deeper.trap: The trap is feeling safe because you know the word. Knowing that outcomes color your judgment doesn't stop them from doing it. So the fix is a habit, not an insight. Write your grade for the idea, the trading and your prep first. Open the P&L only after that.

questions.story: The 2015 Super Bowl. Seattle is down by four on the Patriots' 1-yard line, with 26 seconds left. Coach Pete Carroll calls a pass. It's intercepted, and Seattle loses.
questions.q: How does Annie Duke grade the call?
choices: A sound call with a bad outcome
A bad call, since it lost the game
A bad call, a run was the safe play
No grade until he calls it again
questions.answer: A sound call with a bad outcome
questions.why: A sound call with a bad outcome. Duke calls it mathematically well reasoned. Look at what Carroll knew before the snap. An interception was highly unlikely, and an incomplete pass would have stopped the clock. Most people judged it by the ending, the exact trap Duke names. You don't have to agree with her on the football. The lesson is how she grades it: from the facts at the snap, not from the result. Grade your trades from the moment you clicked.
questions.lesson_line: A well-reasoned call that loses is still well reasoned. Grade your trades the same way.

wrong.A bad call, since it lost the game: That's resulting, the common trap Duke warns about. The interception was the unlikely outcome.
wrong.A bad call, a run was the safe play: Not in Duke's view. An interception was highly unlikely, and an incomplete pass would have stopped the clock.
wrong.No grade until he calls it again: You can grade a call on the odds and the facts at the time. What you can't do is grade it by the result.

questions.simple: Duke calls it sound with a bad result. An interception was very unlikely, and an incomplete pass stops the clock.

deeper.trap: The trap is the vivid ending. The pass was picked off at the 1-yard line and Seattle lost, so the call feels wrong. Duke judges it on what Carroll knew before the snap. He was down four with one timeout. An incomplete pass would stop the clock, and an interception was highly unlikely. Judge the call from there. A trade that stops out works the same way. Judge it from the moment you bought.

questions.story: A stock that's not on your list rips on a headline. You buy at the open with no stop, at double your normal size. It runs, and you sell for your best win of the month.
questions.q: Your best win of the month. Which grades does it fail?
choices: The idea and how you traded it
None, it was your best win
Only the size, the idea was fine
Only your preparation that day
questions.answer: The idea and how you traded it
questions.why: The idea and how you traded it. It wasn't on your list, so no edge from your plan stood behind it. That's the idea grade gone. No stop and double size wreck the trading grade. Every trade we take has a real stop order with the broker, and the size comes from that stop. Tendler says making money with bad process is a step backward. I'd take a clean loss over this win. A win like this can teach you to do it again.
questions.lesson_line: A bad trade that pays is dangerous. It can teach you to do it again.

wrong.None, it was your best win: That's resulting. Winning doesn't fix a missing stop or double size.
wrong.Only the size, the idea was fine: A headline stock that wasn't on your list had no edge from your plan. The idea fails too.
wrong.Only your preparation that day: The story doesn't say how you prepped. The failures came at the click: the idea and how you traded it.

questions.simple: Both fail. The stock was off your plan, with no stop and twice your size.

deeper.trap: The money is real, so it feels like proof. Duke warns that resulting can make bad decisions look worth repeating. Grade it as if it had lost: an off-plan idea, no stop, double size. That grade is low, and the win doesn't change it. The win was luck on top of a bad trade.

questions.q: Over many trades taken the same way, your results start to say something about your process.
questions.why: True. One trade is like a single hand of poker. It says little about the decisions in it. Play enough hands, though, and the results taken together start to tell you something. Trades work the same way. Tendler calls money the scoreboard, just not a reliable one short term. He'd judge P&L over three to six months. That's how we run it. Every month we review the numbers: win rate, average win and loss in R, and expectancy. Each trade I grade on process. The pile I judge on results.
questions.lesson_line: Grade each trade on process. Judge the process on the pile of trades.
questions.simple: True. One trade says little, but many trades taken the same way start to show if your process works.

deeper.counter: The pile only counts if the trades really were taken the same way. Mix breakouts, news trades and dip buys in one total, and the total tells you little about any of them. Results inform you within a run of similar decisions. So keep each setup's trades in their own pile before you judge it.

questions.story: You want a friend's honest read on a trade you took last week. You plan to walk him through it step by step.
questions.q: What do you keep back until he gives his read?
choices: How the trade turned out
Your entry and your stop
Your reasons for the trade
The market at the time
questions.why: How it turned out. Duke reviews a poker hand by putting the listener in her seat at the moment she had to decide. She leaves the result out. Tell him the ending and he'll fit his story to it without meaning to. So give him everything you had when you clicked: your reasons, the market that day, your entry and your stop. Get his grade. Then tell him how it ended.
questions.lesson_line: For an honest grade, hide the ending.

wrong.Your entry and your stop: He needs those to judge the trade. They were part of the decision.
wrong.Your reasons for the trade: That's what he's grading. Hide the result, not the reasons.
wrong.The market at the time: You knew that when you decided, so it belongs in the picture.

questions.simple: Hold back how it turned out. Once he knows the ending, he'll fit his story to it.

deeper.example: Walk him through it the way you saw it when you clicked. Give the setup, why you liked it, the market that day, and your entry, stop and size. Ask for his grade on the idea and on how you planned to trade it. Only then tell him how it ended. If his view shifts once he hears the ending, that shift is the bias at work.

questions.story: Six months, 40 trades on one setup. Almost every trade graded A on process. Taken together, the setup has lost money.
questions.q: What's the pile of trades telling you?
choices: The setup needs a hard look
Nothing, process is what counts
Your grades have been too harsh
Trade it bigger to win it back
questions.answer: The setup needs a hard look
questions.why: The setup needs a hard look. Your process grades say you traded it the way you planned, so execution isn't the problem. Over 40 trades and six months, the results taken together start to talk. A losing run can be bad luck, or it can point to a real problem with the strategy. So check. See whether the setup makes or loses money net, then look for patterns in the winners and the losers. Tag the setup on every trade in your journal, then pull its win rate, average win and loss in R, and expectancy. That doesn't mean drop it tomorrow. It means find out.
questions.lesson_line: Good process can't save a setup with no edge. Over months, the pile of trades shows if yours has one.

wrong.Nothing, process is what counts: Process grades judge each trade. Over months, the results judge the setup.
wrong.Your grades have been too harsh: The grades say you followed the plan. The question now is whether the plan has an edge.
wrong.Trade it bigger to win it back: Sizing up a setup that's losing money makes a possible problem bigger.

questions.simple: The setup needs a hard look. You traded it well, so the losses may point to a setup with no edge.

deeper.trap: The trap is hiding behind good process grades. They judge each trade, and these were good. They can't tell you whether the setup has an edge. The pile of results starts to. Six months is the kind of stretch Tendler means. So the loss deserves a real look: what the winners had in common, and what the losers did.

questions.story: Your reviews show the same thing for weeks. Your idea grades are high, and those ideas often work. But you hesitate, and take few of them, often late.
questions.q: Where should your work go next?
choices: Acting on your own ideas
Finding better trade ideas
More time on morning prep
Taking trades of any kind
questions.why: Acting on your own ideas. Separate grades show you where the leak is, and here it's at the click. Your ideas grade high and they work. You're just not taking them. SMB had this exact problem with probably their highest-P&L trader. Terrific at ideas, trouble pulling the trigger. The work was giving him the confidence to take those trades. A tennis player drills the weak part of the game. Do the same.
questions.lesson_line: Separate grades show you where the leak is. Fix that part, not everything.

wrong.Taking trades of any kind: More random trades would drag your idea grade down. Take the good ones you already find.
wrong.Finding better trade ideas: Your ideas already grade high and often work. Better ones won't help if you don't take them.
wrong.More time on morning prep: Nothing points to prep. The leak is at the click.

questions.simple: Work on acting on your ideas. They already grade well, and the leak is in taking them.

deeper.trap: The trap is fixing what feels comfortable. Hunting for better ideas is fun and feels like work, but your ideas already grade high. A tennis player works on the backhand when the backhand is the weak part, not on the serve. Your separate grades tell you which part of your game that is.

questions.story: You look back at a month of your own trade grades. Every winner got an A. Every loser got a C or worse.
questions.q: What's really going on here?
choices: Your grades are tracking the P&L
You only take truly great trades
Your losers were all just bad trades
Your stops are set much too tight
questions.answer: Your grades are tracking the P&L
questions.why: Your grades are tracking the P&L. Good decisions can end badly, and bad ones can end well. So over a month, some of your losers should be good trades that just lost. Not one A on a loser is the giveaway. The grades are following the money. That's Baron and Hershey's finding again: people rate the thinking as better when the outcome is good. Do it to yourself and you can end up smug after wins and hard on yourself after losses. Write the grade before you look at the P&L.
questions.lesson_line: If my grades always match my P&L, I'm grading the result, not the trade.

wrong.You only take truly great trades: Then some of those great trades would still lose. Not one A-grade loser all month is the giveaway.
wrong.Your losers were all just bad trades: Some losers are good trades that just lost. Every single one being bad is a pattern in your grading.
wrong.Your stops are set much too tight: Tight stops could mean more losers. They don't explain grades that match the P&L every time.

questions.simple: Your grades are tracking the P&L. Good trades sometimes lose, so a month with no good losers points to the grading.

deeper.example: Re-grade a few of the losers without looking at the P&L. Ask only three things: was the idea on plan, were the entry, stop and size right, and were you ready. If some come out as A trades, your first grades were reading the result. Do the same with a few winners. An off-plan win should come out low.

conflicts: The three axes are NOT taught as a UCT house rule. No docs/study house page (sizing_rule.md, TRADE_PLANS.md, OWNER_PRINCIPLES.md) names idea / execution / preparation in the owner's words, and the unit row's source (dossier M12) is docs/curriculum, which is never a source. The same three grades are Brett Steenbarger's published method (SMB video, s1: 'at least three grades for the quality of the ideas that day for the [trading] of those ideas and for my preparation'), so every question names him or asks about the grades as his. Owner: if these are also your three axes, say so in your own words and they can be asked as ours.

s1 is a machine transcript: in f07 it prints 'training of those ideas' where Steenbarger says 'trading'. The same transcript says 'grading that you're trading the idea' (f03), and his own blog lists the same split (s2, s3), so the claim reads it as trading and flags the typo. Quotes were cut only from stretches that read cleanly; the speaker of f08 ('that's an a trade even if ...') is not named in the transcript, so it is credited to SMB's review panel, never to one person.

Steenbarger's own lists differ in detail. The 2020 SMB video gives three daily grades (ideas, trading them, preparation). His 2018 post (s2) gives four separate reviews (ideas, entries and reward for risk, scaling, managing yourself) with no preparation line; his 2019 post (s3) gives ideas, structuring trades, managing risk. They agree on grading the idea apart from how it was traded. The unit keys the three-grade version (the one the unit plan names) and cites s2 / s3 only where they agree.

s1, s2, s3 and s4 are all Steenbarger, and s6, s7 and s8's quotes are all Annie Duke. Where a key rests on two of these, it is a question about that person's own method or view (q01, q04, q06, q07, q09, q11, q23), and the person's own pages are the primary record. Keys that teach a general truth (q02, q08, q10, q14, q17, q19, q20, q22, q24) each pair independent voices: the Baron and Hershey study, Duke, Tendler, Schwab, SMB, WisdomTree.

Results are not worthless, and the file never says they are. Baron and Hershey (f28) say outcomes can inform you across a sequence of similar decisions, Duke (f36) that outcomes in the aggregate over time tell you something, Tendler (f54, f55) that money is the scoreboard over three to six months. The file keys 'one trade's P&L is not its grade' and 'many trades do tell you' (q20, q22); q22 makes the honest flip side explicit (clean process on a losing setup still needs a hard look).

q18: Duke's verdict on the Pete Carroll call (sound decision, bad outcome) is her view and was widely disputed at the time. The question asks how Duke grades it, not whether it was right. Its numbers (26 seconds, 1-yard line, down four, below two percent over 15 years of NFL data) come from the Steve Pomeranz Show's write-up of the book (s9), which is carried on Duke's own site; the Inquirer article (s8) independently confirms the call, the interception and her 'mathematically well-reasoned' judgment.

Resulting vs outcome bias: Duke's word is resulting; the research name is outcome bias (Baron and Hershey, s5; F8.01, F8.03 and F8.05 teach Investopedia's definition). They name the same error. This unit uses 'resulting' as Duke's word (q03, q16, q17) so it does not re-ask F8's definition question.

Overlap with F8, checked: F8.01 q16 and F8.05 q18 already ask 'a rule break that paid' (logged as a mistake), F8.03 q14 asks 'a rules-based trade that hit its stop was not a mistake', and F9.03 q25 asks 'six losses is a tiny sample'. This unit's versions ask which of the three grades fails (q10, q15, q19) and when results do count (q20, q22), so they test a different skill on the same idea.

Baron and Hershey (s5) is a PDF whose line breaks hyphenate some words ('out- comes', 'conse- quences'); the quote checker reads those as two words. Quotes were cut only from unbroken stretches, so f28 starts mid-sentence at 'information can operate only within ...' (the sentence begins 'This effect of outcome information'). The study tested people judging OTHERS' decisions; the paper itself says effects on judging your own are 'suggested' (by dissonance studies), so q24 cites f27 (its own words on judging yourself) for the self-grading line.

Investopedia (outcome bias, risk/reward ratio) refused both the plain client (HTTP 402) and WebFetch on 2026-11-09, so it is not cited. q13's reward-for-risk method rests on Steenbarger (f14 'favorable reward relative to risk'), SMB (f04, chasing into 'poor risk reward') and Schwab's entry-minus-stop example (f58), with the calc.

Checker, 2026-11-09, q18: s9 (the show's write-up) puts a short-pass interception 'below two percent' over 15 years of NFL data, but other retellings of the book give 'about 2%' and the book's own sentence could not be read. Rather than teach a threshold that may be off, q18 now says only that an interception was 'highly unlikely' (s9's own words, f62) and that an incomplete pass stops the clock (f49). f48 stays on file, uncited.

Checker, 2026-11-09: claims shown to members now keep the sources' hedges (f23 'cannot infallibly be graded', f27 and f43 'may' / 'can'), and q16, q19, q24 say 'can' where the source does. q21's story no longer shows 'the chart up to your entry', which gave the answer away.

w1.notes: f07, f02, f04, f05, f06 confirmed in the SMB transcript (2020-11-19), f17 on TraderFeed 2018-10-07, read in context. Step 4 said 'to his own state', which no cited quote says; now 'morning exercise, a look at the markets and a review of the day before', f06's own list.

w2.notes: f29 (Wharton, Duke's words), f34 (Clearer Thinking transcript, Duke answering 'what's resulting'), f44 (Inquirer, Duke quoted) and f08 (SMB panel, said of a trade made on all your checklist criteria) confirmed in context.

w3.notes: f35, f36 confirmed in the Clearer Thinking transcript (outcomes inform 'in the long run'). f54, f55 on Tendler's 'Hating to Lose' (2025-11-10): the plain client got HTTP 502, quotes confirmed with WebFetch; three to six months is his advice to a day trader judging daily P&L, fairly summarised.

q01.notes: Key from f07, f03-f06; choices 29-33 chars, key not longest. Why grounded; 'which part of your game is leaking' is his register. Names Steenbarger by design (lesson conflict: the three axes are his method, not ours).

q02.notes: False from f23, f29, f54. Ends on the practical: grade the idea, entry, stop, size. Hedge kept in simple ('tells you little').

q03.notes: cut in fills: see the resolver's notes

q04.notes: Truth fine (f02). Voice: the verdict 'Was there a real edge in it.' read as a question with a period, the 25-word Steenbarger sentence ran long, and 'Put plainly, was it on your plan...' was stilted. Rewritten: verdict first, sentence split, a straight closing line.

q05.notes: Chasing under the trading grade (f04). 'Chasing costs size' and the 4% line verified verbatim in sizing_rule.md C28 (f67, f73). Wrong notes plain.

q06.notes: True from f06, f16. f68 verified verbatim (F67). One plain claim, no 'but' clause. Practical close: check how you feel before the open.

q07.notes: Chess from f31, f64, f65; f39 for 'more skill, more one result tells you'. 'A trade is a poker hand' lands the point.

q08.notes: Truth: the study tested people judging OTHERS (lesson conflict note); 'So expect your own grades to drift' stated as certain what the source only suggests. Softened to 'can drift', kept the watch-for with a mentor line.

q09.notes: cut in fills: see the resolver's notes

q10.notes: Good trade that lost (f08, f29, f53). Verdict, reason, and 'log it as an A and take the next one the same way' is the how. 'A trade' vs setup-grade letters already an owner flag.

q11.notes: Idea grade low (f02). f69 verified (D39). 'A headline isn't on that list' is his kind of blunt line.

q12.notes: Truth fine: f66 matches B22 verbatim, 3 and 5R cited. Added where to find it (rule 14: earnings dates on the UCT Terminal calendar) and tightened the opening so the reason (knowable ahead) leads.

q13.notes: Recomputed: (56-53)/(53-48) = 3/5 = 0.60 (key). Distractors: plan (56-50)/(50-48) = 3.00; flipped 5/3 = 1.67; mixed (56-50)/(53-48) = 1.20. All match their wrong notes. One overstatement: $53 is 6% over $50, two points past the 4% line, so 'well past it' became 'past it'.

q14.notes: Key from f24, f25, f37. Researchers named because the question is about their finding (rule 13). Practical: go back to where you stood when you clicked.

q15.notes: Exit grade (f09, f10, f05). Story is about breaking your own sell plan, not a fixed trim rule, so it does not misstate the first-sell ruling.

q16.notes: Other half from f52; f43 for 'bad decisions reinforced'. 'Break a rule, get paid, call it skill' is good. Wrong notes plain.

q17.notes: False from f26; f40, f38. f70 verified (B27). The how (grade before you look at the P&L) is in why, simple and lesson line.

q18.notes: Duke's verdict (f45, f62, f49, f47). No 2% figure. 'You don't have to agree with her on the football' keeps the disputed call honest.

q19.notes: Idea and trading fail (f02, f04, f56). f71 verified (D41). 'I'd take a clean loss over this win' is his register.
